prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps) implements Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) under International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance for National Airspace System (NAS) Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)/airspace users negotiate assigned closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current-state-to-destination. Aircraft comply within tolerances and share predicted intent; controllers retain separation responsibility, without routine self-separation. Automation distributes changes to affected users, aircraft and FAA systems. NAS Constraint Service publishes static/dynamic constraints. Traffic management automation translates traffic management initiatives (TMIs) into traceable flight-specific constraints. Negotiating controllers subsume D-side duties; traffic management coordinators (TMCs) support traffic flow management (TFM).
TFM selects TMIs; MBT assigns/updates compliant trajectories. Near-term Ground Delay Programs (GDPs)/Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) remain; longer-term Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) replaces Expect Departure Clearance Time (EDCT) constraints. Operators choose takeoff times balancing speed, CTA compliance and other constraints. Mile-in-trail/minute-in-trail (MINIT) restrictions decrease, eventually disappearing with time-constrained 4DTs. Increased self-separation techniques (A-IM, unexpanded) support merging without repeated time-constraint updates. Closed trajectories deconflicted for at least 30 minutes may increase sector capacity.
Near-term System Wide Information Management (SWIM) extensions support mixed equipage; far-term Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2) supports digital trajectories/Flight Management System (FMS) loading; voice remains. Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) exchanges clearances/intent. FMS supports one active Required Time of Arrival (RTA). Required Time Performance (RTP) certification is mandatory without RTA; RTP-Y specifies crossing-time-error 95% confidence interval, seconds, distribution-independent, for TOAC constraints; complements Required Navigation Performance (RNP).
Surface MBT is normally excluded; surface/en-route data exchange must ensure trajectory consistency with predicted takeoff/landing times, runways and transitions.
Reduced uncertainty/predictability-based scheduling may reduce flexibility, increasing fragility to residual uncertainty. Research must validate TFM adaptation; conservative initial delay absorption followed by incremental delay release can require repeated trajectory updates.

U0112: Definitions This chapter presents definitions and discussions of key terminology and concepts. 2.1 Trajectory In the context of MBT, a three-dimensional trajectory (3DT) is a description of an aircraft’s path in space.
U0113: A 3DT is often visualized as a string or tube through space, and described by two dimensions in a horizontal plane (e.g., longitude and latitude) and one vertical dimension (the aircraft’s altitude).
